posts.title: Measuring your carbon footprint: Scope 1, 2 and 3 explained
posts.excerpt: The three scopes of greenhouse gas emissions, in plain language, with Kenyan examples of what goes where.
posts.html:
Greenhouse gas emissions are grouped into three scopes under the GHG Protocol.

Scope 1: what you burn

Fuel in your vehicles, generators and boilers. For many Kenyan businesses, diesel for backup power is the largest item.

Scope 2: the electricity you buy

Power from Kenya Power. Kenya's grid is largely renewable, so Scope 2 is often smaller here than elsewhere.

Scope 3: everything else in your value chain

Purchased goods, transport, business travel, waste and the use of your products. It is usually the largest and hardest to measure, so start with the biggest categories.

posts.title: eTIMS: why your expenses may not be deductible without a valid tax invoice
posts.excerpt: Since KRA tied expense deductions to electronic tax invoices, a missing eTIMS invoice can cost you the deduction. Here is what to check.
posts.html:
KRA now expects most business expenses to be supported by an electronic tax invoice generated through eTIMS. Where a supplier cannot give you one, the expense may be disallowed when your income tax return is reviewed, even if the money was genuinely spent.

Who this affects

Any business that claims expenses against its income, and any supplier that sells to businesses. Small suppliers, landlords and service providers who are not yet on eTIMS are the most common gap.

What to do now

  • List your regular suppliers and check which of them issue eTIMS invoices.
  • Ask non-compliant suppliers to register, or plan to use the buyer-initiated invoice option where it applies.
  • Check that the invoice details match your PIN exactly.
  • Keep invoices with your books, not in an inbox.

How we can help

We review your expense records, flag the invoices that would not survive a KRA review and set up a simple routine to keep you covered every month.

posts.title: Case analysis: input VAT and a supplier who did not declare the sale
posts.excerpt: Sample analysis. The Tribunal considered whether a buyer loses its input VAT claim when the supplier fails to declare the sale.
posts.html:
This sample shows the layout of a case analysis. Replace it with a real decision before launch.

The decision is a reminder that the burden of proof in tax disputes sits with the taxpayer, and that it can be discharged with ordinary business records. Data-matching reports are a starting point for KRA's enquiries, not proof on their own.

Businesses should treat supplier due diligence as part of their VAT routine: a PIN check, a copy of the supplier's registration, and documents that show the goods or services actually changed hands.

meta.case_name: Sample Trading Limited v Commissioner of Domestic Taxes
meta.case_means:
Keep evidence that goods or services were actually supplied, not just the invoice.
Check new suppliers on the KRA PIN checker before you buy.
Respond to KRA's data-matching queries with documents, not explanations.
meta.case_issues:
- Whether the taxpayer was entitled to claim input VAT on purchases from a supplier who had not declared the sales.
- Whether the Commissioner was right to rely only on a data-matching report.
meta.case_facts:
The taxpayer claimed input VAT on purchases from a registered supplier. KRA's systems showed that the supplier had not declared the corresponding sales, and the Commissioner disallowed the claims.

The taxpayer produced invoices, delivery notes, bank payments and stock records showing that the goods were received and used in the business.
meta.case_decision: The Tribunal allowed the appeal. It held that a buyer who proves that a genuine supply took place, and that it paid for it, should not lose its input VAT because of the supplier's failure to declare. The Commissioner's remedy lay against the supplier.

posts.title: Materiality: deciding what to report
posts.excerpt: You cannot report on everything. A materiality assessment tells you what matters most to your business and your stakeholders.
posts.html:
Materiality is the filter that keeps a sustainability report focused. A topic is material if it could reasonably affect decisions made by the people who use your report.

Single and double materiality

IFRS S1 and S2 look at how sustainability matters affect the business: its cash flows, access to finance and cost of capital. The GRI Standards look the other way, at the business's impact on people and the environment. Doing both is called double materiality.

A simple process

  • List possible topics, using your sector and the questions you receive.
  • Ask stakeholders which matter to them.
  • Score each topic for impact and financial effect.
  • Agree the final list with your board.

posts.title: ESG reporting in Kenya: where to start
posts.excerpt: Who is asking for ESG information, what they want to see, and the first three steps for an organisation starting from zero.
posts.html:
ESG reporting can feel like a new language. It is really a structured way of answering questions your stakeholders are already asking: how do you affect the environment, how do you treat people, and how is the business run?

Who is asking

  • Lenders and development finance institutions, as a condition of funding.
  • Export buyers, especially in Europe, through supplier questionnaires.
  • Investors, boards and, for listed companies, the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

Three first steps

  • Name one person to own ESG reporting.
  • List the ESG questions you have already been asked.
  • Gather the data you already have: energy bills, fuel, staff numbers, policies.

In the next part of this series we look at materiality: how to decide what is worth reporting.

posts.title: Case analysis: deductibility of management fees paid to a related company
posts.excerpt: Sample analysis. The High Court considered what evidence is needed to deduct management fees paid within a group.
posts.html:
This sample shows the layout of a case analysis. Replace it with a real decision before launch.

Groups that charge management or technical fees between companies should assume KRA will ask what was delivered. The best evidence is created at the time: reports, emails, meeting notes and a clear basis for the amount charged.

meta.case_name: Example Holdings Limited v Commissioner of Domestic Taxes
meta.case_citation: Income Tax Appeal No. E000 of 2025 (sample)
meta.case_means:
Document what a related company actually does for its fee.
Keep a transfer pricing policy and benchmark the charge.
A contract alone will not prove that a service was provided.
meta.case_issues: - Whether management fees paid to a related company were wholly and exclusively incurred in the production of income.
meta.case_facts: The taxpayer deducted management fees paid to its parent company under a group services agreement. The Commissioner disallowed the deduction because there was no evidence of the services actually delivered.
meta.case_decision: The Court dismissed the appeal. A services agreement and invoices were not enough without evidence of the services themselves, such as reports, correspondence and time records.

posts.title: What lenders are asking about ESG, and how to answer
posts.excerpt: Banks with sustainability commitments now screen borrowers. The questions are predictable, and so are the answers that work.
posts.html:
If you have applied for finance recently, you may have met an environmental and social questionnaire. Lenders use them to manage their own risks and commitments.

Common questions

  • Do you have environmental, health and safety policies?
  • How do you manage waste and emissions?
  • What are your labour practices, including for contractors?
  • Who in the business is responsible for ESG?

Honest, documented answers beat polished ones. Where you have gaps, say what you are doing about them.

posts.title: Five tax deadlines Kenyan businesses miss most often
posts.excerpt: Instalment tax, withholding VAT and annual returns catch out even well-run businesses. A short list to pin on the wall.
posts.html:
Most penalties we see are not about complicated tax. They are about dates.

The usual suspects

  • Monthly PAYE, VAT and withholding tax returns and payments.
  • Instalment tax, paid during the year rather than at the end.
  • The annual corporate income tax return, six months after the year end.
  • Rental income tax for landlords.
  • Annual returns at the Business Registration Service, which are not a KRA filing but carry their own penalties.

A simple fix

Put every date in one calendar, with a reminder a week before. Our clients get one, with their own dates filled in.

posts.title: A plain guide to SHIF, NSSF and the Housing Levy for employers
posts.excerpt: What each statutory deduction is for, who pays it and when it is due.
posts.html:
Every Kenyan employer deducts several statutory amounts from pay. Getting them right protects your staff and your business.

The main deductions

  • PAYE: income tax on employment income.
  • SHIF: contributions to the Social Health Insurance Fund.
  • NSSF: pension contributions, shared by employer and employee.
  • Affordable Housing Levy: shared by employer and employee.

Rates and caps change, so check the current figures each year or let us handle it for you.

posts.title: Case analysis: withholding tax on services from a non-resident
posts.excerpt: Sample analysis. The Court of Appeal considered when payments to a non-resident are subject to withholding tax.
posts.html:
This sample shows the layout of a case analysis. Replace it with a real decision before launch.

Payments abroad are a frequent source of KRA assessments. A short check before each payment avoids most of them.

meta.case_name: Illustrative Services Limited v Commissioner of Domestic Taxes
meta.case_means:
Check withholding tax before paying any foreign supplier.
Tax treaties can reduce the rate, but only with the right documents.
Penalties can be challenged even where the tax itself is due.
meta.case_issues:
- Whether payments to a non-resident for services were subject to withholding tax.
- Whether penalties and interest should apply.
meta.case_facts: The taxpayer paid a foreign company for software support without deducting withholding tax. The Commissioner assessed the tax with penalties and interest.
meta.case_decision: The Court upheld the tax but set aside part of the penalties, finding that the taxpayer had acted on a reasonable reading of the law at the time.

posts.title: Choosing the right business structure in Kenya
posts.excerpt: Sole proprietorship, partnership, LLP or limited company: what each means for liability, tax and paperwork.
posts.html:
The structure you choose affects your personal liability, how you are taxed and what you must file each year.

The options

  • Sole proprietorship: simple, but you are personally liable.
  • Partnership: shared ownership, shared liability.
  • Limited liability partnership: partnership flexibility with limited liability.
  • Private limited company: a separate legal person, preferred by lenders and investors.

There is no single right answer. It depends on your plans, your risks and who you will need to convince.

legal.privacy:
This policy explains how JENIQA Advisory Limited ("we", "us") collects, uses and protects personal data through this website, in line with the Data Protection Act, 2019 of Kenya and its regulations.

## Who we are

JENIQA Advisory Limited is the data controller for personal data collected through this website. You can contact us using the details on our contact page.

## What we collect

- Details you give us in our forms: your name, organisation, email address, phone number, the service you are interested in and your message.
- Your email address if you subscribe to our newsletter.
- Basic technical data needed to run the website securely, such as your IP address, browser type and the pages you visit.

## Why we use it

- To respond to your enquiry or proposal request, which is the lawful basis of taking steps at your request before entering into a contract.
- To send you our newsletter, with your consent. You can unsubscribe at any time.
- To keep the website secure and working, which is in our legitimate interests.

## How long we keep it

We keep enquiries for up to two years unless they lead to an engagement, in which case our engagement records policy applies. Newsletter subscriptions are kept until you unsubscribe.

## Who we share it with

We do not sell personal data. We share it only with service providers who help us run the website and email, under contracts that protect it, or where the law requires it. Some providers may store data outside Kenya; where they do, we make sure appropriate safeguards are in place as the Act requires.

## Your rights

Under the Data Protection Act you have the right to be informed of how your data is used, to access it, to object to its processing, to have it corrected or deleted, and to data portability. To exercise these rights, contact us. You may also complain to the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner.

## Changes

We may update this policy. The date at the bottom of the page shows when it last changed.
legal.cookies:
Cookies are small files a website stores on your device. This page explains how this website uses them.

## Essential only

This website does not set advertising or tracking cookies. Our hosting provider may set short-lived technical cookies that keep the site fast and secure. They do not identify you personally.

## Analytics

If we add privacy-friendly visit statistics, they count page views without cookies and without identifying you. If that ever changes, we will ask for your consent first and update this page.

## Maps

## Managing cookies

Most browsers let you block or delete cookies in their settings.
